newsitem.title: USA: High-speed train project seen boosting Florida.
newsitem.headline: High-speed train project seen boosting Florida.

text.p: A plan to link Florida's major cities with a $5.3 billion high-speed railway system would be an economic boon for the state over the next 45 years, researchers studying the plan said Tuesday.
In all, construction and operation of a 320-mile system linking Tampa, Orlando and Miami would result in the creation of 250,000 jobs and nearly $9 billion in wages over the next 40 years, it said.

The indirect financial benefits would be even more significant, pumping nearly $35 billion in additional economic activity into Florida's economy over the next four decades, while saving lives and reducing stress on Florida's already clogged roadways and airways.

"This project is going to have a significant impact on Florida's economy and it's going to be across the entire state with the largest focus being along the travel corridor," said Tim Lynch, researcher at the Florida State University Center for Economic Forecasting and Analysis and co-author of the report.

The study, which was conducted in cooperation with the University of South Florida's Center for Urban Transportation Research, countered a rival analysis released in April by The James Madison Institute, a conservative Tallahassee-based think tank.
That study, conducted by the Wendell Cox Consultancy, said such a system would be a "financial disaster" that could cost Florida taxpayers $40 billion.
As proposed, the system would include a 320-mile network of electrified high speed rail lines connecting seven terminals between Tampa, Orlando and Miami.
Travelers on the system, which is modeled after the French TGV high speed system, would be whisked from Tampa to Miami in two and a half hours.

In 1996, Florida transportation officials awarded the franchise to Florida Overland eXpress, an Orlando-based consortium of transportation companies led by Fluor Daniel, Odebrecht Contractors of Florida, GEC Alsthom, and Bombardier. FOX beat out five other bidders for the franchise.
Under the agreement, Florida will pump in $70 million a year to help fund the project, with FOX kicking in $349 million.

The rest must come from federally-backed bonds, a critical link that has yet to be finalized. Company officials said Tuesday they will await the conclusion of separate ridership studies and corridor acquisition studies before deciding whether to proceed with the franchise agreement.
Tuesday's upbeat analysis, however, was viewed as a positive first step.

"At the end of the day, as private companies, we're going to go forward with this partnership if the studies prove it to be a very basic, solid business decision," said FOX CEO David Gedney. "We're all looking forward to the results"
